Comparing models and brains Georgia Institute of Technology

Representational Similarity Analysis

A representation is a shape. Two systems with different neurons, units, and numbers of dimensions can still be compared, because a shape is fully described by the distances between the things it contains.

N. Apurva Ratan Murty, PhD
Assistant Professor, School of Psychological and Brain Sciences · Georgia Tech
murtylab.com ↗

Content check by Mainak Deb, Alish Dipani, and Nikolas McNeal

We want to compare what is happening inside a brain with what is happening inside a model. But the two systems represent an image in very different spaces: a brain region gives us a pattern of activity across voxels, while a network layer gives us a pattern of activity across units. How can we compare them?

We will first consider a geometric picture, as given by a popular approach called representational similarity analysis (Kriegeskorte, Mur & Bandettini, 2008, Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience). Rather than asking whether individual voxels correspond to individual units, we ask how stimuli are arranged relative to one another in each representational space. Which images are represented similarly? Which are represented differently? And does the same geometry emerge in the brain and the model?

01Geometry

The intuition

Images that are close by are "similar" in brain or model space.

Imagine a brain region responding to different pictures. We can represent each picture as a point: pictures that produce similar patterns of brain activity are placed close together, while pictures that produce different patterns are placed farther apart.

The map below shows this for ten pictures. The table next to it contains exactly the same information in numerical form. Each entry gives the distance between a pair of pictures. This table is called a representational dissimilarity matrix, or RDM.

Show
Distances are scaled so the farthest pair is 1. In dissimilarity mode farther apart is darker; the diagonal is zero. Toggle to similarity and each cell becomes 1 − d, so the diagonal is 1 and closer pairs are darker. Either way the matrix is symmetric and holds 45 distinct numbers. Hover a cell to see which pair it belongs to.

Those 45 numbers are the geometry. They tell us how far every picture is from every other picture. If we know all of those distances, we can reconstruct the arrangement of the pictures. The whole map could be rotated or flipped and nothing important would change: the relationships among the pictures would remain exactly the same.

That is what makes an RDM useful. It captures the geometry of a representation without caring about the particular coordinates used to draw it.

Drag the mouse next to the elephant. Which cells change? Now press Sort by size. The table reorganizes into a different block pattern because the map now groups pictures by a different property.

02Dimensions

Real spaces have many axes

Nobody can draw a map with 200 axes. Distance is defined in any number of them.

Suppose we record from just three neurons. Each picture produces three responses, one from each neuron. Those three numbers become the picture's coordinates, placing it at a point in a three-dimensional space. Pictures that produce similar patterns of neural activity will lie close together; pictures that produce different patterns will lie farther apart.

The logic is exactly the same as before. We can measure the distance between every pair of pictures and collect those distances into an RDM. The only thing that has changed is the number of dimensions: each distance is now determined by the responses of three neurons rather than two.

Each axis is one neuron. Rotating the view changes every coordinate on the screen and changes nothing in the table on the right: the distances between points do not depend on where you stand. Hover a cell to highlight that pair in the space.

Suppose we record responses to the same set of pictures from 500 neurons. Each picture gives us 500 numbers, one response from each neuron. Together, those numbers place the picture at a point in a 500-dimensional space. We cannot physically draw that space, but we can still get an intuition for its structure from the geometric relationships among the pictures. Pictures that evoke similar patterns of activity will be close together; pictures that evoke different patterns will be farther apart. Measure the distance between every pair of pictures, and we have an RDM.

We can do this with almost any kind of brain measurement. With fMRI, the dimensions might be voxels. With EEG or MEG, they might be electrodes or sensors at a particular moment in time. With ECoG, they might be electrodes on the cortical surface. The measurements change, but the logic does not. Each picture produces a pattern of responses, and the distances between those patterns tell us about the geometry of the brain's representation.

Now take a neural network. The logic is exactly the same. Think of a layer with 2,048 units as recording from 2,048 artificial neurons at once. Each picture produces 2,048 responses and therefore becomes a point in a 2,048-dimensional space. Again, we cannot draw that space, but we can measure the distances between pictures. Do this for every pair, and we have an RDM for the network.

Here is what we gain. The brain might have 500 measurements and the network 2,048. There is no reason that neuron 7 should correspond to unit 7, or that any individual dimensions should correspond at all. But the pictures are the same. So rather than trying to match individual neurons to individual units, we can ask whether the two systems arrange those pictures in similar ways.

Representational similarity analysis, or RSA, is the similarity between these two RDMs. If pictures that are close together in the brain are also close together in the network, and pictures that are far apart in the brain are also far apart in the network, the two RDMs will be similar. The RSA score measures that agreement, giving us a way to compare the internal representations of two systems even when their underlying dimensions are completely different.

Distance
Each row is one picture; each column is one voxel or unit (red positive, blue negative). Hover a cell for its value. The distance menu changes the rule used to compare two rows; the panel at the bottom works one pair through by hand. Correlation distance ignores how strongly a picture drives the region overall and keeps only the pattern across voxels. It is the usual choice for fMRI.

Each picture is a vector, $\mathbf{x}_i$, with one entry per neuron. Any rule that turns two vectors into a distance will do. Four common choices:

Correlation distance · the usual choice for fMRI
$$d_{ij} \;=\; 1 - r\!\left(\xi,\ \xj\right), \qquad r \;=\; \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n} \big(\xik-\xbi\big)\big(\xjk-\xbj\big)} {\sqrt{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\big(\xik-\xbi\big)^{2}}\;\sqrt{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\big(\xjk-\xbj\big)^{2}}}$$
$\xi$ and $\xj$ are the response vectors of the two pictures; $\xbi$, $\xbj$ their means across the $n$ neurons. $r$ runs from $-1$ to $1$, so $d$ runs from $0$ to $2$.
Euclidean distance
$$d_{ij} \;=\; \big\lVert\, \xi - \xj \,\big\rVert_2 \;=\; \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{n} \big(\xik-\xjk\big)^{2}}$$
The straight-line distance between the two points, exactly as on the maps above. Sensitive to the overall level of response as well as its pattern.
City-block (Manhattan) distance
$$d_{ij} \;=\; \big\lVert\, \xi - \xj \,\big\rVert_1 \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{n} \big|\,\xik-\xjk\,\big|$$
Add up the absolute differences neuron by neuron. Less dominated by a single neuron with a very large difference than the Euclidean rule.
Mahalanobis distance · Euclidean after whitening the noise
$$d_{ij} \;=\; \sqrt{\big(\xi - \xj\big)^{\!\top}\, \Sigma^{-1}\, \big(\xi - \xj\big)}$$
$\Sigma$ is the noise covariance of the neurons, estimated from repeated measurements. Neurons that are noisy, or whose noise is shared with other neurons, count for less. With $\Sigma = I$ the rule is Euclidean. The cross-validated version, computed across independent runs so that noise cannot inflate it, is called the crossnobis distance (Walther et al., 2016, NeuroImage) and is the current default in many fMRI RSA pipelines.

Correlation distance ignores how strongly a picture drives the region overall and keeps only the pattern across neurons. Euclidean and city-block distance keep the overall level as well. The sum runs over the $k$ neurons, whether there are 3, 500, or 2,048 of them.

In Python the whole RDM is one line. With the responses in an array X of shape (pictures, neurons):

# X: responses, one row per picture, one column per neuron
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist, squareform

rdm = squareform(pdist(X, metric='correlation'))   # 1 - r
rdm = squareform(pdist(X, metric='euclidean'))
rdm = squareform(pdist(X, metric='cityblock'))
rdm = squareform(pdist(X, metric='mahalanobis', VI=np.linalg.inv(Sigma)))   # Sigma: noise covariance

# one pair by hand, e.g. pictures 0 and 1
r = np.corrcoef(X[0], X[1])[0, 1]
d = 1 - r

pdist returns the 45 distances of the lower triangle as a vector, in the same order as the CSV download above; squareform folds them into the $10 \times 10$ matrix.

The last step is the score itself. Take the 45 distances above the diagonal of each RDM and correlate them. The RSA score is a rank correlation: identical geometry gives 1, unrelated geometry gives about 0.

RSA score
$$\rho_{AB} \;=\; \operatorname{Spearman}\!\Big(\operatorname{upper}(D_A),\ \operatorname{upper}(D_B)\Big) \;=\; 1 - \frac{6\sum_{p=1}^{m} \big(R^A_p - R^B_p\big)^{2}}{m\,(m^{2}-1)}$$
$D_A$ and $D_B$ are the two RDMs; $\operatorname{upper}(\cdot)$ takes the $m = n(n-1)/2$ entries above the diagonal (here $m = 45$); $R^A_p$ and $R^B_p$ are the ranks of pair $p$ in each. The right-hand form holds when there are no ties.

Ranks are used rather than raw distances because we do not expect distance in a brain and distance in a network to be on the same scale, or even linearly related. Only the ordering of pairs is asked to agree. If elephant and dog are the closest pair in the brain, they should be among the closest pairs in the model.

⚠ What a high score does not mean

A high RSA score says the two systems have the same geometry. It does not say they use the same axes, and it does not say they compute the same features. Two systems can have identical RDMs and share no single dimension in common: rotate or mirror the map in Figure 1 and every distance, and therefore the score, stays exactly the same.

👉 Try it

Switch between layers. Early layers of a network tend to be organized by low-level image properties, later layers by category. The simulated brain region cares about animacy and size, so it matches some layers better than others.

03Hypotheses

Models as hypotheses

Any claim about what a region cares about can be written as an RDM and scored.

An RDM does not have to come from measurements. "This region separates animals from objects" is a matrix with 0 for same-kind pairs and 1 for different-kind pairs. "This region sorts by real-world size" is another. Each hypothesis is scored the same way as a network layer. Every candidate is on the same footing: a network layer, a hand-written hypothesis, a different brain region, another subject. Whatever it is, it becomes a $10 \times 10$ RDM over the same pictures, and it gets one number.

04Noise

How high can the score go?

The brain does not agree perfectly with itself. No model should be expected to do better than that.

Even a perfect model should not be expected to reach an RSA score of 1, because brain measurements are noisy. One way to see this is to measure the same brain region twice, build an RDM from each measurement, and correlate the two RDMs. Even though they come from the same region, the correlation will be less than perfect.

Often, we estimate this using a split-half correlation. Take the brain data and divide the measurements into two independent halves, for example odd and even runs. Average the responses within each half, build one RDM from each, and correlate the two RDMs. That correlation tells us how well the brain agrees with itself.

This reliability helps establish the noise ceiling: the level of agreement we can reasonably expect given the noise in the measurements. So if a model does not reach an RSA score of 1, that is not necessarily a failure. The meaningful question is how close the model gets to the reliability of the brain data themselves.

Figure 5 — Model scores against the noise ceiling
Interactive · slider
Measurement noise0.4
The gold bar is the score of the brain against a second run of itself. Turn the noise up: the ceiling drops, and so does every model's score, because the same noise sits in the brain RDM they are compared with.
Reading a score

A model that scores 0.55 against a ceiling of 0.6 is nearly as good as the data allow. A model that scores 0.55 against a ceiling of 0.95 is missing most of the structure. Always report the ceiling next to the score.

05Procedure

The whole method in four steps

Same pictures, one RDM per system, one correlation, one ceiling.

To compare two systems with RSA, the recipe is straightforward.

  1. Show the same set of pictures to every system you want to compare. These could be two brain regions, two people, two species, or a brain and a neural network.
  2. Build an RDM for each system. Take the response to each picture and compute its distance from the response to every other picture. Because every system saw the same pictures, all of the RDMs have exactly the same size, even though the underlying measurements might be completely different.
  3. Compare the RDMs. Take the unique entries from each matrix, usually one half of the matrix above the diagonal, and correlate them. Often we use a rank correlation such as Spearman correlation. If pairs of pictures that are far apart in one system also tend to be far apart in the other, the correlation will be high. That correlation is the RSA score.
  4. Establish the noise ceiling. We need to know how good that score could possibly be. Brain measurements are noisy, so even two measurements of the same brain will not agree perfectly. We can estimate this reliability from repeated measurements or independent splits of the data. The noise ceiling gives us a reference for interpreting how much of the measurable representational structure a model captures.
06Neuroscience

Early results with RSA

One of the first demonstrations of RSA compared object representations in monkey and human IT cortex. Kriegeskorte and colleagues showed the same 92 object images to two macaques and four humans. In the monkeys, they recorded from 674 individual neurons in inferotemporal (IT) cortex, a high-level visual region involved in object recognition. In the humans, they measured activity across 316 IT voxels using fMRI.

These are very different kinds of measurements. There is no sensible way to say that a particular neuron in the monkey corresponds to a particular voxel in the human. But both experiments used the same 92 pictures. So the authors built an RDM for each species and compared the two RDMs.

And the structure was strikingly similar. In both species, animate objects separated from inanimate objects, and within the animate objects, faces and bodies formed distinct clusters. The measurements were completely different, but the geometry was similar: monkey and human IT arranged the same pictures in similar ways (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008, Neuron; open access).

Figure 6 — Monkey IT and human IT arrange the same 92 images the same way

Neuron 2008
View
Reproduced from Kriegeskorte et al. (2008). RDMs for monkey IT (left, 674 neurons) and human IT (right, 316 voxels). Images are ordered animate then inanimate, with faces and bodies grouped within animate; color is the percentile of 1 − r, blue near, red far. The animate and inanimate blocks, and the face sub-block inside animate, appear in both species.

Can a model reproduce the brain's representational geometry?

The second result asked whether a computational model could reproduce this geometry. Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte tested 37 models, ranging from hand-designed vision features such as GIST and SIFT, to neuroscience-inspired models such as HMAX, to a deep convolutional neural network trained on ImageNet.

For each model, they showed the same images, built an RDM from its internal responses, and compared that RDM with the one measured in human IT. Which model arranged the images most like the human brain?

Most of the hand-built and unsupervised models captured relatively little of IT's categorical structure. The supervised deep network did much better, and the match to IT increased across layers, with the later layers showing the strongest similarity.

The result was important because the comparison did not require individual model units to correspond to individual voxels. The model was successful because the geometry of its representation increasingly resembled the geometry measured in human IT (Khaligh-Razavi & Kriegeskorte, 2014, PLOS Computational Biology; open access).

Figure 7 — A deep network's RDMs, layer by layer, against IT
From the paper
PLoS Comput Biol 2014
Reproduced from Khaligh-Razavi & Kriegeskorte (2014), CC BY. RDMs of the same 92 images computed from each layer of a deep convolutional network trained on ImageNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Under each matrix is its agreement with human IT and monkey IT (Kendall's τA, a rank correlation like Spearman's). Agreement rises through the convolutional layers and peaks in the fully connected layers 6 and 7, where the animate block in the upper left emerges clearly. The final class-score layer drops again: it is organized by ImageNet labels rather than by the categorical divisions IT cares about.

The two results are the same argument twice. RSA let neurons be compared with voxels because both reduce to a geometry over the same images. It then let a network's units be compared with those voxels for the same reason. The units of measurement change; the RDM does not care.

Concept Check

Test your understanding

Answer these questions to test your concepts.

Your score
Part 1 complete · vocabulary checklist
01 · Representation

A shape

Where each stimulus sits relative to the others. Described completely by pairwise distances.

02 · RDM

$D_{ij} = d(\xi, \xj)$

Symmetric, zero diagonal, $n(n-1)/2$ distinct entries. The same size for every system.

03 · Invariance

Axes drop out

Rotation, reflection, and scale leave the RDM unchanged. So does the number of dimensions.

04 · RSA score

Spearman of upper triangles

Rank correlation between two RDMs. 1 means identical geometry, 0 means unrelated.

05 · Model RDM

A hypothesis as a matrix

Category labels, feature norms, or a network layer. All are scored the same way.

06 · Noise ceiling

Brain vs itself

The score between two runs of the same data. The bar no model can reliably clear.

07 · Evidence

Monkey, human, network

IT geometry matches across species (2008) and is reproduced by supervised deep nets (2014).

Part 2 asks a directional question. Instead of comparing two geometries, an encoding model fits weights from a network layer to each voxel and is judged by how well it predicts responses to images it never saw. RSA tells you the shapes match. Encoding models tell you which features do the work.
